title: Does residual load explain German day-ahead electricity prices on a year the model never saw, and how wrong was the flat merit-order price?
summary: Fits price as a non-decreasing function of residual load (load minus solar minus onshore wind) by isotonic regression on hourly German day-ahead prices 2015–2019 (OPSD/ENTSO-E), and scores it on a held-out year. Trained on 2015–2018 and tested on 2019: correlation 0.87 and RMSE 9.6 EUR/MWh, against 14.5 for an hour-of-day mean, 15.7 for the training mean and 23.0 for the flat EUR 54.6/MWh merit-order price of energy-thermal-hourly. Leave-one-year-out over all five years gives correlation 0.78–0.90 and beats every non-residual baseline in every year; the flat model is worse than the training mean in four of five. The predicted cheapest-quarter mean, which is what a storage buyer pays, is within EUR 3.7–9.2/MWh of the actual one. Most of the remaining error is the yearly price level (fuel and carbon), not shape: an oracle level cuts RMSE to 6.2–11.2. No data after 2019 (hosts unreachable from the run container); one held-out year per score, no confidence interval; realised rather than forecast load and renewables; onshore wind and solar only. All inputs are from sources.
lede: does residual load explain German day-ahead prices on a year the model never saw? Yes: correlation 0.87 and RMSE 9.6 EUR/MWh on 2019 against 23.0 for the flat merit-order price; the cheap-quarter mean is within EUR 4–9/MWh; the rest is the fuel-price level.
